belt: Hi — I'm ready to start Define on our project.

reply.answer:
Welcome — I'm here to coach you and your team through your improvement project step by step, so you don't need to be an expert. We'll work through five phases together:
• Define — pin down the problem and who's solving it
• Measure — get the real numbers
• Analyse — find the true root cause
• Improve — test and apply the fix
• Control — make the gains stick
Right now we're in Define — the most important phase, because a clear problem is half the solution. For each of the thirteen parts I'll explain what it is and why it matters, show you a finished example, then ask for yours. When all thirteen are agreed, you and your team review the Define report and approve it.

Let's start with the first part: the business case.

The business case says why this project deserves time and people: what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and what it costs. It is what earns the project its support. People outside the team only back what they can understand and size — and it is the first thing the Define report shows.

Here’s an illustration of a business case — this is an example, not your data: “During January to June 2026, 12% of invoices produced by UK billing were returned for correction, against 3% for the rest of the group. The rework and delayed payments cost about €35k a month.”

Why is your project worth doing? Tell me what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and roughly what it costs.
reply.explanation: The business case explains why the project deserves time and resources, showing what is wrong, where and since when, how big it is, and what it costs.
reply.example: “During January to June 2026, 12% of invoices produced by UK billing were returned for correction, against 3% for the rest of the group. The rework and delayed payments cost about €35k a month.”
reply.prompt: Why is your project worth doing? Tell me what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and roughly what it costs.

In your case, you mentioned 23% of invoices were paid late during January to June 2026. Is this your baseline? If so, please confirm or provide the correct number.

Let's move forward to the next part of the Define phase: the project team.

The project team identifies who leads, sponsors, owns the process, and does the work — each with a name, a role, and what they will do. A project needs people before it needs work. The champion clears obstacles, and the process owner keeps the result after the project ends; without them, a good fix fades.

Here’s an illustration of a project team — this is an example, not your data:
"Leader: Anna (Green Belt, runs the project). Champion: Mark, Finance Director (approves, removes blockers). Process owner: Jo, Billing Manager (owns the process). Members: two billing clerks (know the work). Training: the clerks need a half-day on data collection before Measure."

Now let's move on to the next part of the Define phase: the Voice of the Customer (VOC).

The Voice of the Customer identifies who receives what your process produces — inside the company, outside, or both — what they need, and the Critical-to-Quality requirements (CTQs): each need turned into something you can measure. This keeps the project honest, ensuring we improve what matters to the people receiving the output. A CTQ is how "they want it accurate" becomes a requirement you can check.

Here’s an illustration of a VOC summary — this is an example, not your data: "Customers: client finance teams (external) and our credit control (internal). They need invoices that are correct and on time; the top complaint is wrong amounts. CTQs: invoice amount matches the agreed price on 100% of lines; invoice sent within 2 working days of the order."

Who are the customers of your process, and what do they need or complain about most? For each need, how would you measure that it is met?
reply.explanation: The Voice of the Customer identifies who receives your process outputs, what they need, and measurable requirements (CTQs) to ensure those needs are met.

Now let's move on to the next part of the Define phase: the benefits analysis. This identifies what the gap costs today (the cost of poor quality, or COPQ), whether the gain is sustainable (every year) or one-off, when the money will be realised, and who in finance validates the figure. It establishes the value of the project in terms finance will accept — a figure checked by finance is one the champion can defend.

Here’s an illustration of a benefits analysis — this is an example, not your data: "Cost of the gap: about €11k a year in rework (4,200 invoices, 12% → 3%, about €30 each), from the savings calculation. Impact: sustainable — reduced cost every year. Realisation: from Q4 2026, about €2.7k a quarter. Finance contact: Priya Shah, management accountant."

Next, the cost of the gap needs to be calculated. This translates the gap you are closing into an annual money figure: (the baseline rate − the target rate) × how many units go through in a year × what one defect costs. Cutting errors from 12% to 3% on about 4,200 invoices a year, at about €30 to put each one right, is roughly €11k a year.

To run the calculation, I need two numbers from you: roughly what one defect costs (with its currency) and how many invoices you handle a year.

This is a one-page, high-level map of the process as it runs today: Suppliers give Inputs; the Process, in four to eight main steps from start to end, turns them into Outputs, which go to Customers; and what is measured on those outputs. It puts the whole process on one page, so the team agrees where it starts and ends and who it serves. It maps the process as it IS, not as it should be — an ideal map hides the problem.

Here’s an illustration of a completed SIPOC — this is an example, not your data:

| Suppliers | Inputs | Process | Outputs | Customers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sales team | Signed order | 1. Receive order | Invoice (PDF) | Client finance team |
| Pricing database | Price list | 2. Look up prices | Payment request | Credit control |
| Client | Client details | 3. Generate invoice | Audit record | |
| | | 4. Review and approve | | |
| | | 5. Send to client | | |

How each part is formulated: suppliers are who provides; inputs and outputs are things (nouns); each process step starts with a verb; customers are who receives the outputs. Measured on the outputs: invoice error rate, cycle time.

reply.answer:
Welcome to Measure. Quick recap of what Define locked in, so we're building on the same picture:

• **Problem:** Across our three hospital sites, 23% of supplier invoices were paid after their 30-day terms from January to June 2026. Suppliers chase us by phone and email, and some put us on stop, delaying stock for ward managers. Late payments cost us interest, lost discounts, and supplier trust.
• **Baseline:** One metric: late payment rate, in %, meaning the share of supplier invoices paid more than 30 days after the invoice date. It is about 23% today, from the AP ledger for January to June 2026. It feeds our finance KPI, creditor days.
• **Target:** Late payment rate: under 5% of supplier invoices by 31 March 2027, and keep it under 5% for three months after that.
• **Process (SIPOC):** Suppliers: our medical and general suppliers, and the purchasing team who raise the purchase orders. Inputs: supplier invoices, purchase orders and goods-received notes. Process: receive the invoice, match it to the purchase order and the goods receipt, resolve mismatches, approve, then schedule and release payment. Outputs: paid invoices and remittance advice. Customers: the suppliers, and our ward managers who rely on their deliveries. Process metrics: days from invoice receipt to payment release, and the share of invoices with a match exception.

Now, what Measure actually does: we expand that SIPOC into a detailed process map, decide what to collect and how, check the measurement itself can be trusted, confirm the process is behaving consistently, establish a real baseline, and prioritise which inputs are most likely driving the problem. You don't need to hold these in a fixed order in your head — I'll guide you — but here's the full menu so nothing's a surprise:

**Required (7)**
□ Detailed process map — timings, people, value vs waste per step
□ Data collection plan — what, how much, how often, who
□ Stability check — is the process behaving consistently?
□ Baseline — the current level, once we trust the data
□ Cause prioritisation — scoring what might be driving it
□ Vital few X's — the shortlist Analyse will test
□ Issues and barriers — what's in your way

**Recommended (3)**
□ Sigma level · □ Measurement system check · □ Secondary metrics

**Progress: 0 of 7 required complete**

We'll work through these roughly in the order above, and I'll flag the two recommended ones — the measurement system check and the sigma level — when we reach them, rather than saving them for the end. First up: expanding your Define map, because everything else attaches to it. Let me show you what that looks like.

metric_definitions.name: late_payment_rate
metric_definitions.meaning: The share of supplier invoices paid more than 30 days after the invoice date

baseline_estimate.raw: One metric: late payment rate, in %, meaning the share of supplier invoices paid more than 30 days after the invoice date. It is about 23% today, from the AP ledger for January to June 2026. It feeds our finance KPI, creditor days.

target_value.raw: Late payment rate: under 5% of supplier invoices.

result.calculation_note: (23% baseline − 5% target) × 42000 units/year × 9 per unit = 68040 a year. Check the units agree: the rates are shares of the yearly volume, and the unit cost is the cost of one defect.
